body.text: On August 7, three countries—Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan—signed the “Makkah Joint Defence Agreement”, based on “the enduring bonds of brotherhood and Islamic solidarity that unite them” and on their interest in “building upon their shared strategic interests and long-standing defence cooperation”. The agreement, the three nations said, was towards “further strengthening their collective security and… promoting peace, security, and stability in the region and beyond”.

The agreement emerged after discussions between the Foreign Ministers of Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, Pakistan, and Egypt took place on three occasions in recent months, with senior officials meeting before the conclaves to give substance and direction to the high-level discussions. A Turkish official said that the agreement had been under consideration for over two years and eight months, confirming that the conflicts in West Asia from late 2023 onwards had influenced the major states to explore new arrangements to protect their shared security interests.

Leaders and spokespersons of the three countries hastened to affirm that the agreement was defensive and not directed at any specific country. A senior Saudi official dealing with public affairs clarified: “The agreement does not represent any intention to build a military axis or a sectarian/religious bloc [and is] not linked to nuclear ambitions or an arms race, but rather to building sustainable, self-reliant capabilities.”

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said the agreement was based on “collective deterrence” and assured the international community that Türkiye would continue “its principled stance towards resolving conflicts and crises through dialogue and diplomacy on the basis of respect for international law”. The Pakistani Foreign Office affirmed that, in terms of the agreement, an attack on any member would be regarded as an attack on all and that the agreement was “intended to strengthen collective deterrence”. A Jordanian commentator described the agreement as “a signal flare built into a joint security network”.

The three-party coalition brings together considerable potential capability in terms of Saudi energy and finances and Türkiye’s strong defence industry, particularly in drones and munitions systems, and its familiarity with state-of-the-art military equipment due to its NATO membership. Pakistan has long-standing and close political and military ties with both Saudi Arabia and Türkiye and has a large and well-equipped military force, besides nuclear capability. According to an Al Jazeera report, Pakistan has had close military ties with Saudi forces for decades, while Türkiye and Pakistan have exchanged warships and training aircraft. In 2023, Saudi Arabia agreed to buy Turkish drones in what Türkiye described as its largest defence export contract.

The agreement is expected to include training, exchange of personnel, joint exercises, intelligence sharing, and, above all, mutual defence. Obviously, there will no automatic deployment of troops in the event of a military crisis; there will be joint consultations to decide on the line of action. The promoters also note that it provides for collective self-defence as envisaged in the UN Charter.
Saudi security concerns

What led to this dramatic agreement? First, Saudi security concerns. From the early days of the Arab Spring 15 years ago, Saudi Arabia has been aware that the US can no longer be relied upon as the regional security guarantor. Besides publicly discussing a possible “pivot” to the Asia-Pacific in response to China’s rise, in 2015 the Barack Obama administration finalised without consulting the regional states a nuclear agreement with Iran, an agreement promising to relax sanctions on Iran and give it an unrestricted role in the region. Even though the US under Donald Trump later withdrew from the agreement, it failed to protect the interests of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states when their tankers, oil facilities, and other assets were attacked by Iran or its proxies.

Saudi Arabia had then attempted to shape a select military alliance, with some joint exercises in March 2016. About 20 countries from West Asia, Asia, and Africa participated in these exercises that involved military aircraft, helicopters, and tanks. Named “North Thunder” and described as “the largest military in the region’s history”, the exercises took place as tensions mounted with Iran and Saudi Arabia engaged with Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen.

A year later, in January 2017, Saudi Arabia announced the appointment of the former Pakistani army chief General Raheel Sharif as head of the Islamic Military Counter Terrorism Coalition (IMCTC), which several observers referred to as a “Muslim NATO”. The general was selected largely on account of his record in confronting militants in Pakistan. Several commentators viewed the IMCTC as an anti-Shia coalition. While its website suggests that its 43-member body continues to meet regularly and even has a GCC military officer as Secretary General, there has since been no news about any significant role it has played in the region.
What went wrong?

By the end of 2020, after the US failed repeatedly to provide security to the region and was unable to mobilise Islamic countries into a robust military coalition, Saudi Arabia acknowledged the need to rebuild ties with Iran. Between 2021 and 2022, there were five rounds of dialogue between the two in Baghdad. These were suspended in early 2022 due to domestic political issues in Iraq.

In December 2022, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is reported to have sought the help of Chinese President Xi Jinping to bring the two estranged neighbours together. China’s mediation worked: in March 2023, a Saudi-Iranian rapprochement was announced in Beijing, which involved the establishment of full diplomatic ties and substantial security and economic engagement.

However, Saudi Arabia and its GCC partners did not get much time to enjoy a sense of regional security. Within seven months, the Hamas attacks on Israel and Israel’s counter-attacks on Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon, and Iran, with periodic assaults in Iraq and Yemen, pulled the GCC states into the quagmire. Again, Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping closed that crucial waterway during most of 2023–25, while US-Israeli attacks on Iran in June 2025 led to a counter-attack on US facilities in Qatar.

However, it was the Israeli air attack on Doha on September 7, 2025, that brought the ongoing West Asian conflict directly to the GCC states. Israel declared that its attacks were directed at Hamas officials in Doha negotiating peace proposals via Qatar. However, the GCC states themselves and most commentators understood the attacks to be a signal from Israel that it was the regional military hegemon and no regional target was safe from it. Within a few days of the Doha attack, Saudi Arabia entered into a mutual defence pact with Pakistan, while Qatar itself sought security guarantees from the US.

But worse was to follow. Once the US and Israel began direct attacks on Iran from February 28, 2026, Iran retaliated with missile and drone attacks on US targets across the region, but primarily in the GCC. Within the first few weeks, there were several hundred Iranian attacks. These were directed at GCC targets and hit, besides US assets, local energy, infrastructure, industrial, communications, and hi-tech facilities.

In Saudi Arabia, the Prince Sultan airbase with American aircraft was attacked several times, alongside energy facilities and civilian airports. In September 2025, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif reminded Iran of Pakistan’s mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia and moved 13,000 troops and several aircraft to Saudi Arabia, but there were no reports of any Pakistani action. To complicate the situation, the Houthis in Yemen also launched missiles on Saudi targets in Yemen itself and on Najran in south-western Saudi Arabia, even as pro-Iran militants in Iraq attacked the kingdom with missiles.

Iran’s attacks revealed another serious vulnerability in the region: the rapid depletion of interceptors. In the first five weeks of the conflict, the UAE intercepted nearly 550 ballistic missiles, about 2,300 drones, and 26 cruise missiles, while Saudi Arabia intercepted nearly 900 aerial threats. Saudi Arabia deployed about 2,400 PAC-3 interceptors, using up 86 per cent of its pre-war inventory. The US did no better, using up about 65 per cent of its Patriot interceptor stockpile and 38 per cent of its THAAD reserves, even redeploying batteries from South Korea despite serious objections from the latter. This situation convinced GCC states to reduce their dependence on the US and diversify defence partnerships.

Additionally, Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz dealt a severe blow to energy exports by GCC states. Saudi Arabia responded by sending its oil exports by pipeline from the Eastern Province to Yanbu port on the Red Sea, which took care of about 70 per cent of its normal exports. It also launched retaliatory attacks on targets in Iraq and Yemen but ducked a major regional escalation of conflict by avoiding direct attacks on Iran.

Saudi Arabia blames the US for the conflict expanding across West Asia. Besides providing full support to Israel, the US joined Israel in attacking Iran despite warnings from GCC states to avoid war and give ongoing negotiations a chance. A recent media report quoted a GCC official as saying: “Trump started this war, and we are paying the price.”
The cost of prioritising Israel

From Saudi Arabia’s perspective, the conflict is the result of the US continuously prioritising Israel’s interests over those of its GCC partners. This recalls the US-led war on Iraq in 2003, largely promoted by Israel, which had the unintended consequences of expanding Iranian influence in Iraq and encouraging the rise of the transnational extremist entity the Islamic State.

The latest defence agreement is a result of increasing Saudi disenchantment with the US’ role in West Asia and its total loss of credibility as a regional security provider. Having said this, none of the three partners is envisaging a break from the US; each cherishes ties with it in political, security, economic, and technology areas and sees no reason to disrupt them at this stage.

As the commentator Andreas Krieg explained: “Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan… are building the capacity to protect their interests when Washington cannot or will not do so. Riyadh wants several layers of security rather than one American umbrella.”

The three countries are now building the foundation for a new alliance that accommodates their diverse interests while recognising that a solid security partnership will take time and effort. The grouping is thus a long way from an “Islamic NATO”, which will need a joint command centre, a common budget, and a permanent military force. These might emerge over time when new members are taken in and shared security and military doctrines finalised.

Some signals have already come from Türkiye: a week after the agreement, Ankara said the pact would soon be placed on a “more institutional and sustainable” footing, to include “strategic, political and military mechanisms… involving Defence Ministers, Foreign Ministers and Chiefs of General Staff/Armed Forces Commanders”. Joint military exercises and air defence and unmanned systems are planned, alongside deeper defence industry cooperation. Another report from Türkiye spoke of plans to set up a political and military committee and a secretariat in Saudi Arabia.

Given the free hand the US, Israel, and Iran have enjoyed in regional affairs thus far, this tripartite grouping presents itself as a new force and a potential constraint on the actions of these other players. The regional expert H.A. Hellyer believes the pact “sends a politically symbolic signal to Iran and Israel”.

Others see Iran as an obvious target, with some imparting it a sectarian character on the lines of the Saudi effort to confront Iran and its proxies in 2016. In fact, an expert on Saudi Arabia, Umar Karim, said the alignment “is clearly oriented towards Iran and meant to address Iran’s new strategic approach geared towards dominance of the broader Gulf region”. However, while commentators may be focussing on Iran, possibly to obtain US backing for the coalition, the principal security threat the three partners share is from Israel, whose far-right government has wreaked extraordinary death and destruction across the region, with senior Israeli leaders publicly saying Türkiye will be the next target.

One commentator noted that Israel’s “appetite for grabbing Palestinian and Arab territory has grown unchecked” and needs to be confronted by regional states. Israel’s attacks across the region, particularly on Iran, have heightened security concerns in Türkiye, which has its own ambitions for West Asia and the western Indian Ocean. It is interesting to note that Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi welcomed the agreement. The Minister tweeted: “When Muslims stand together, we can face every challenge by malicious outsiders head-on. Time to rely only on ourselves and embrace true brotherhood.”

Trump, too, welcomed the Makkah agreement, writing on Truth Social: “It shows how the Middle East is coming together, and how countries will finally be able to defend themselves in a more meaningful manner.”
Concerns for India

For India, the nascent coalition poses several concerns, primarily the lead military role played by Pakistan and the expansion of Pakistan’s presence in West Asian affairs over the past year, particularly its ties with Türkiye. Türkiye has reportedly been providing Pakistan with modern military equipment such as armed UAVs, precision-guided munitions, stealth-oriented corvette warships, and electronic countermeasure technologies.

There are concerns in India that Pakistan’s participation in the coalition has brought West Asian conflicts to its doorstep. Pakistan’s earlier role in Western alliances provided it with military equipment that it used against India. Pakistan has also enjoyed considerable political and diplomatic support from its Western allies, particularly the US, including the West’s blind eye to Pakistan-sponsored cross-border terror against India.

Some commentators believe that India’s deepening ties with the UAE and Israel might be a strategic nexus against the Makkah alignment. They cite India’s participation in the I2U2 (India, Israel, UAE, US) partnership, its support of the India-Middle East-Europe Corridor, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Israel on the eve of the Iran war.

This is a rather superficial and simplistic reading. The Makkah agreement is deeply anchored in West Asia’s contentions and, despite Pakistan’s participation, is unlikely to be directed at India. Also, India has long-standing ties with Saudi Arabia, which is home to one of the largest Indian diasporas, and India is expected to be a major buyer of Saudi oil over the next few decades.

However, it would be wrong to believe that South Asia can remain insulated from West Asia, with which it has ties that go back several millennia. The Cambridge scholar Ved Shinde has pointed out that the security of South Asia and West Asia is closely linked, a point that was noted during Prime Minister Indira Gandhi’s visit to Saudi Arabia in 1982 and repeated after Modi’s visit in 2016.

The new alliance calls for a new approach in India’s engagement with West Asia: a shift from bilateral and transactional ties to collective interaction with the region as a whole. Through the recent war, India has largely stayed aloof despite having crucial stakes in the region’s stability. Simultaneously, other countries have actively pursued political and military options to safeguard their interests, such as the Makkah pact. However, there is still scope for course correction. India should actively engage with leaders across West Asia to promote peace and long-term security arrangements. India’s absence has given other states the space to pursue engagements that are not necessarily in India’s interests, such as a military alliance made on the basis of Islamic identity.

The Makkah coalition has been consciously shaped in “Islamic” terms: the signing took place in the holy spot of Makkah among three states anchored in Islam: Saudi Arabia as guardian of its holy shrines, Pakistan as inheritor of South Asia’s Islamic heritage, and Türkiye with its Ottoman legacy. Can this underpinning be the basis for the revival of Islamic power? The record in this regard is not particularly impressive: despite several references to pan-Islamism over the last two centuries, there is no evidence of Islamic states coming together with shared interests in any area such as Palestine or even to jointly celebrate Muslim culture and achievement.

There is no doubt that in coming weeks there will be several references to political solidarity based on Islam, with new states joining on this basis, but the earlier Organization of Islamic Cooperation serves as a warning: in its five-decade history, it has absolutely nothing to show for its efforts.

History shows that alignments founded on faith have not been particularly resilient, nor are they likely to meet a better fate in the contemporary era. The most effective political orders are those that unite their people at home and give them a shared sense of national purpose and commitment.

Talmiz Ahmad is former ambassador to Oman, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia and is Distinguished Professor for International Studies, Symbiosis International University, Pune. A new edition of his book West Asia at War (2022) is expected in the next few months.
